title: Statistical priming and signal decomposition for repeatable throughput
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures an experiment-first methodology for making throughput benchmarks repeatable by treating warmup/priming as a statistical signal decomposition problem. Notes, heuristics, and a concrete checklist for bench runs are here. Mostly rough — keeping as a lab notebook rather than a canonical playbook (yet).

Context and motivation:
- We repeatedly see run-to-run variance even when hardware, model, and load profiles match. Noise sources: GPU microstates, scheduler jitter, thermal throttling, memory fragmentation, lazy kernel compilation, KV-cache cold misses, and client-side pacing variability.
- Existing heuristics (fixed N requests warmup) sometimes under- or over-prime depending on workload occupancy, sequence length skew, and batching effects. Need principled way to decide warmup length and to measure when the system is "statistically primed."

Core idea (high level):
- Treat the observed throughput/latency time series as the superposition of: (1) slow drift (thermal/alloc), (2) step-change priming transients (compilations, cache fill), (3) high-frequency noise (jitter), and (4) workload signal (user pattern).
- Use short exploratory runs to estimate transient timescales, then design priming windows to remove transient bias and stabilize measurement windows. Prefer robust summary stats (median/trimmed mean + bootstrap CI) rather than raw mean.

Quick experiment template (to run before any benchmark):
1) Exploratory probe (20–60s): low-rate steady arrival matching expected occupancy. Capture 1s-resolution throughput, GPU util, power, and kernel compilation events.
2) Compute: rolling mean/median with windows {5s, 15s, 60s}; compute change-point detection (CUSUM or simple slope) to find when throughput stops rising consistently.
3) Estimate priming time Tp = earliest t such that subsequent 60s window has slope magnitude < 0.5%/s and throughput variance stabilizes below threshold. Record Tp.
4) Use Tp to select warmup budget for production runs: warmup = min(max(2*Tp, 30s), 5m) — double to be conservative but cap for practical reasons.

Loadgen config recommendations (bench-runner flags and rationale):
- run_duration: 900  # total run 15m (allows warmup + measurement)
- arrival_pattern: poisson  # reduces artificial synchronization
- mean_qps: X  # set to target occupancy-derived qps
- seed: multiple seeds (see repeatability below)
- measurement_window: 60  # measure in 60s sliding windows after warmup
- client_threads: keep small (4–8), prefer many lightweight coroutines to avoid host-level jitter
- sampling_resolution: 1s  # 1s time buckets for throughput/latency traces

Repeatability matrix and seeds:
- For each benchmark config, run at least: 5 seeds x 3 thermal states = 15 runs. Seeds: list of rand seeds for request ids/arrival RNGs (do not reuse the same client thread–seed mapping repeatedly).
- Thermal states: cold (idle 30m), warm (idle 5m), hot (sustained load 10m before run). This surfaces thermal hysteresis.
- Use different rng seeds for arrival inter-arrival times and payload/noise selection. Track seeds in metadata.

Stabilization metrics (what we use to assert "stable measurement window"):
- Throughput CV (coefficient of variation) over measurement window < 2.5% (configurable by SLA)
- p95 latency drift from window start to end < 5% relative
- GPU stall ratio and SM occupancy plateau (internal telemetry) change < 1–2% over window
- No kernel JIT events reported during measurement window (if JITs occur, discard run)

Signal decomposition checklist (practical steps during capture):
- Plot time series: throughput, median latency, p95 latency, GPU temp/power, nvprof/kernels if available.
- Mark events: model load, first batch compile, large-allocation GC, KV-cache first read, heavy page faults. Label these on timeline.
- Apply 3 smoothing scales to throughput (fast: 5s, mid: 30s, slow: 120s) and compute deltas. If fast->mid reduction > 10% in first 2m, we likely have lingering priming effects.

Special priming modes (workload-specific):
- KV-cache heavy workloads: add explicit synthetic prefix sequences during warmup to populate cache. Use representative prefixes sampled from production token distribution.
- Quantized paths: force a few short seqs that exercise quant-dequant kernels during warmup (some kernels only executed for certain token lengths).
- Multi-model fanout: sequentially prime each model instance, then run a short mixed fanout probe to exercise scheduler multiplexing.

Failure modes and how to triage quickly:
- Run shows sudden drop mid-measurement: check GPU power/thermal alarms and host-level preemption logs. If host preemption, mark run invalid and escalate to infra.
- High variance with no visible kernel or thermal events: suspect client-side pacing jitter — increase client threads and add byte-level pacing randomness.
- Persistent upward drift across many runs: revisit lazy kernel compile instrumentation; capture nvprof traces on single short-run to identify missing kernels.

Reporting and summary statistics (what we publish):
- For each benchmark target: median throughput and 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples) from the measurement windows across seeds and thermal states.
- p50/p95/p99 latency distributions aggregated the same way. Report trimmed-mean throughput (drop top & bottom 5% samples) as robustness check.
- Include a short-run "artifact trace" (1s-resolution time series) for auditing results and regression debugging.

Practical run checklist (copy-paste for bench operator):
- [ ] Note run config + bench-runner commit + git rev for model artifact
- [ ] Ensure GPU drivers and CUDA are pinned to test baseline
- [ ] Ensure no background batch jobs; check node housekeeping cron windows
- [ ] Run exploratory probe and compute Tp per template above
- [ ] Set warmup = clamp(2*Tp, 30s, 5m) in bench-runner config
- [ ] Run bench set: seeds = [list], thermal = [cold,warm,hot]
- [ ] After each run: collect /var/log/syslog, dmesg, nvidia-smi --query, bench traces, and git metadata
- [ ] Discard runs with JIT events in measurement window; re-run with updated warmup

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to automatically detect kernel JITs reliably from remote telemetry without nvprof? (we see symbols but not JIT markers in prod)
- Is doubling Tp conservative enough for large-scale multi-tenant clusters? need cluster-level experiments.
- Investigate lightweight online detection: can the runtime emit a "primed" event when KV cache and kernel warm counters exceed thresholds? Design proposal needed.

Planned follow-up experiments (short list):
- A/B: fixed warmup 60s vs adaptive Tp-based warmup across 100 runs to quantify CI shrinkage and re-run rate due to JITs.
- Priming-only microbenchmark: targeted sequences that exercise all known kernel variants (token lengths 8/32/128/512) to enumerate missing-to-warm kernels.
- Client-side pacing stress: replace Poisson with client-level burst patterns to see sensitivity and derive recommended client pacing heuristics.

Notes to self (scratchpad):
- capture seeds in bench-runner metadata: add --metadata-json field if not present
- consider adding thermal state tag to Prom labels so we can quickly filter runs in observability
- remember to add link to INF-1427 when writing final playbook

Appendix: example bench-runner invocation (shell-friendly):
bench-runner --run-duration 900 --arrival-pattern poisson --mean-qps 1200 --seed-list 42,123,987,2025,31415 --measurement-window 60 --client-threads 6 --warmup 120 --out artifact-20250302.json

End notes: keep this doc informal until we validate the adaptive-Tp heuristic across 100+ runs. If it stabilizes CI and reduces re-run rate, move upstream to the official "priming best practices" doc and add a runtime signal hook for "primed" events.
